claim: SRSF1 is essential for gene expression and splicing in mouse SSCs.
source: We demonstrated that SRSF1 is essential for gene expression and splicing in mouse SSCs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Spermatogonia-related genes (e.g. Plzf, Id4, Setdb1, Stra8, Tial1/Tiar, Bcas2, Ddx5, Srsf10, Uhrf1, and Bud31) were bound by SRSF1 in the mouse testes.
source: Crosslinking immunoprecipitation and sequencing data revealed that spermatogonia-related genes (e.g. Plzf, Id4, Setdb1, Stra8, Tial1/Tiar, Bcas2, Ddx5, Srsf10, Uhrf1, and Bud31) were bound by SRSF1 in the mouse testes.
evidence: This claim is supported by CLIP-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Specific deletion of Srsf1 in mouse germ cells impairs homing of precursor SSCs leading to male infertility.
source: Specific deletion of Srsf1 in mouse germ cells impairs homing of precursor SSCs leading to male infertility.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Germ cells are absent in the testes of adult conditional knockout (cKO) mice.
source: Whole-mount staining data showed the absence of germ cells in the testes of adult conditional knockout (cKO) mice, which indicates Sertoli cell-only syndrome in cKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount staining experimental data.

claim: cKO mice exhibit Sertoli cell-only syndrome.
source: Whole-mount staining data showed the absence of germ cells in the testes of adult conditional knockout (cKO) mice, which indicates Sertoli cell-only syndrome in cKO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of germ cells shown by whole-mount staining data.

claim: The expression of spermatogonia-related genes (e.g. Gfra1, Pou5f1, Plzf, Dnd1, Stra8, and Taf4b) was significantly reduced in the testes of cKO mice.
source: The expression of spermatogonia-related genes (e.g. Gfra1, Pou5f1, Plzf, Dnd1, Stra8, and Taf4b) was significantly reduced in the testes of cKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SRSF1 may affect survival of spermatogonia by directly binding and regulating Tial1/Tiar expression through AS.
source: Moreover, multiomics analysis suggests that SRSF1 may affect survival of spermatogonia by directly binding and regulating Tial1/Tiar expression through AS.
evidence: This is suggested by multiomics analysis combining CLIP-seq, RNA-seq, and AS analysis data.

claim: SRSF1 interacts with RNA splicing-related proteins (e.g. SART1, RBM15, and SRSF10).
source: In addition, immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation data showed that SRSF1 interacts with RNA splicing-related proteins (e.g. SART1, RBM15, and SRSF10).
evidence: This is supported by IP-MS and Co-IP experimental data.

claim: SCOS is one of the most common causes of severe non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA).
source: Sertoli cell-only syndrome (SCOS), also known as del Castillo syndrome or germ cell aplasia, is one of the most common causes of severe non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2023.

claim: SCOS is the presence of only Sertoli cells in the testicular tubules of the testes, with no germ cells present.
source: SCOS is the presence of only Sertoli cells in the testicular tubules of the testes, with no germ cells present (Juul et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Juul et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2023.

claim: Abnormal self-renewal and differentiation of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) lead to SCOS.
source: It is well known that abnormal self-renewal and differentiation of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) lead to SCOS (Kanatsu-Shinohara and Shinohara, 2013; La and Hobbs, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanatsu-Shinohara and Shinohara, 2013 and La and Hobbs, 2019.

claim: In mice, gonocytes begin homing at 0–3 days postpartum (dpp) and then develop into SSCs at 4–6 dpp for continuous self-renewal and differentiation.
source: In mice, gonocytes begin homing at 0–3 days postpartum (dpp) and then develop into SSCs at 4–6 dpp for continuous self-renewal and differentiation (Lee and Shinohara, 2011; McLean et al., 2003; Tan and Wilkinson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee and Shinohara, 2011; McLean et al., 2003; and Tan and Wilkinson, 2020.

claim: Homing of precursor SSCs is crucial for forming SSC pools and establishing niches.
source: The mechanisms regulating homing of precursor SSCs are hence crucial for forming SSC pools and establishing niches (Oatley and Brinster, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oatley and Brinster, 2012.

claim: Spermatogonia migrate to form two distinct subtypes in mice.
source: Spermatogonia migrate to form two distinct subtypes in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The first subtype of spermatogonia develops into precursor SSCs that provide an SSC population for adult spermatogenesis.
source: The first subtype develops into precursor SSCs that provide an SSC population for adult spermatogenesis, whereas the second subtype transitions directly to differentiated spermatogonia that contribute to the first round of spermatogenesis but do not self-renew (Kluin and de Rooij, 1981; Law et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kluin and de Rooij, 1981 and Law et al., 2019.

claim: The second subtype of spermatogonia transitions directly to differentiated spermatogonia that contribute to the first round of spermatogenesis but do not self-renew.
source: The first subtype develops into precursor SSCs that provide an SSC population for adult spermatogenesis, whereas the second subtype transitions directly to differentiated spermatogonia that contribute to the first round of spermatogenesis but do not self-renew (Kluin and de Rooij, 1981; Law et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kluin and de Rooij, 1981 and Law et al., 2019.

claim: Many transcription factors (e.g. FOXO1, PLZF, POU5F1, TAF4B, CHD4, BCL6B, BRACHYURY, ETV5, ID4, LHX1, POU3F1, DMRT1, NGN3, SOHLH1, SOHLH2, SOX3, and STAT3) promote SSC self-renewal and differentiation.
source: Many transcription factors (e.g. FOXO1, PLZF, POU5F1, TAF4B, CHD4, BCL6B, BRACHYURY, ETV5, ID4, LHX1, POU3F1, DMRT1, NGN3, SOHLH1, SOHLH2, SOX3, and STAT3) promote SSC self-renewal and differentiation (Cafe et al., 2021; Song and Wilkinson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cafe et al., 2021 and Song and Wilkinson, 2014.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of the posttranscriptional network underlying homing of precursor SSCs are not sufficiently clear.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms of the posttranscriptional network underlying homing of precursor SSCs are not sufficiently clear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: DND1 and DDX5 are key RNA-binding proteins in SSCs with a unique and dominant role in posttranscriptional regulation.
source: Previous studies have identified the key RNA-binding proteins DND1 and DDX5 in SSCs with a unique and dominant role in posttranscriptional regulation (Legrand et al., 2019; Yamaji et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Legrand et al., 2019 and Yamaji et al., 2017.

claim: The RNA-binding proteins SRSF10, UHRF1, BUD31, and BCAS2 regulate alternative splicing (AS) in mouse spermatogonia.
source: Surprisingly, recent studies have found that the RNA-binding proteins SRSF10, UHRF1, BUD31, and BCAS2 regulate alternative splicing (AS) in mouse spermatogonia (Liu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2023; and Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: Testes are rich in AS events.
source: It is well known that testes are rich in AS events (Mazin et al., 2021; Venables, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mazin et al., 2021 and Venables, 2002.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of how AS functions in homing of precursor SSCs are still largely unclear.
source: However, the underlying mechanisms of how AS functions in homing of precursor SSCs are still largely unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: SRSF1 is a widely studied and important splicing factor involved in cancer progression, heart development, and thymus development.
source: Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 1 (SRSF1, previously SF2/ASF) is a widely studied and important splicing factor involved in cancer progression, heart development, and thymus development (Du et al., 2021; Katsuyama et al., 2019; Katsuyama and Moulton, 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Du et al., 2021; Katsuyama et al., 2019; Katsuyama and Moulton, 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2021; and Xu et al., 2005.

claim: SRSF1 deficiency impairs primordial follicle formation during meiotic prophase I and leads to primary ovarian insufficiency.
source: Our previous work has shown that SRSF1 deficiency impairs primordial follicle formation during meiotic prophase I and leads to primary ovarian insufficiency (Sun et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2023b, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: The underlying mechanisms by which SRSF1 regulates pre-mRNA splicing in mouse SSCs remain unknown.
source: However, the underlying mechanisms by which SRSF1 regulates pre-mRNA splicing in mouse SSCs remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: SRSF1 was expressed during spermatogenesis.
source: Fascinatingly, the results of SRSF1 and γH2AX co-staining revealed that SRSF1 was expressed during spermatogenesis (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of SRSF1 fluctuated during the developmental stages of the testes.
source: RT-qPCR and western blotting results showed that the expression of SRSF1 fluctuated during the developmental stages of the testes (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and western blotting data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: SRSF1 was highly expressed in the nuclei of spermatogonia.
source: Concurrently, the results of SRSF1 and PLZF co-staining revealed that SRSF1 was highly expressed in the nuclei of spermatogonia (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by co-staining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Spermatogenesis-related genes were regulated by SRSF1.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analyses of the SRSF1 peak-containing genes revealed that spermatogenesis-related genes were regulated by SRSF1 (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis of CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Global Srsf1 knockout is lethal in mice.
source: Considering that global Srsf1 knockout is lethal in mice (Xu et al., 2005), we used a conditional allele of Srsf1 (Srsf1Fl) in which exons 2, 3, and 4 of Srsf1 are flanked by two loxP sites (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2005.

claim: Vasa-Cre Srsf1Fl/del mice have Srsf1 deletion in germ cells.
source: By crossing Srsf1Fl and Vasa-Cre mice, we obtained Vasa-Cre Srsf1Fl/del mice with Srsf1 deletion in germ cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the breeding strategy and genotyping data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The SRSF1 protein is absent in germ cells of cKO mice.
source: We verified the absence of the SRSF1 protein in germ cells by co-immunofluorescence analyses with SRSF1 and PLZF antibodies (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: cKO mice had a standard mating capacity but the absence of Srsf1 led to complete infertility in males.
source: Subsequently, the breeding experiment indicated that conditional knockout (cKO) mice had a standard mating capacity but that the absence of Srsf1 led to complete infertility in males (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by fertility test data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Sperm could not be found in the cauda epididymis of cKO mice.
source: Histological examination of cKO epididymides revealed that sperm could not be found in the cauda epididymis (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The adult cKO mice were normal in size.
source: The adult cKO mice were normal in size (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by body size and weight data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The sizes of cKO mouse testes were significantly reduced.
source: However, the sizes of cKO mouse testes were significantly reduced (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by testis size and weight data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: No germ cells could be visualised in the testes of cKO mice, and only a large number of Sertoli cells were observed.
source: Histological examination of cKO testis sections showed that no germ cells could be visualised, and only a large number of Sertoli cells were observed in the testes of cKO mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: SRSF1 is critical for spermatogenesis and its absence leads to SCOS.
source: Together, these results demonstrated that SRSF1 is critical for spermatogenesis and that its absence leads to SCOS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: SRSF1 deficiency impaired germ cell survival.
source: These data suggested that SRSF1 deficiency impaired germ cell survival (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by PLZF and γH2AX co-staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Germ cells were indeed absent in the testes of adult cKO mice.
source: Considering the limitations of sectioning, we used whole-mount immunostaining to perform a comprehensive analysis and found that germ cells were indeed absent in the testes of adult cKO mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The testes of 7 dpp and 14 dpp cKO mice were much smaller than those of Ctrl mice.
source: Morphological results showed that the testes of 7 dpp and 14 dpp cKO mice were much smaller than those of Ctrl mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Germ cells were still present in cKO mice but were significantly reduced in 7 dpp and 14 dpp cKO testes.
source: The results showed that germ cells were still present in cKO mice but were significantly reduced in 7 dpp and 14 dpp cKO testes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by VASA staining data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Apoptosis significantly increased in cKO testes.
source: In addition, TUNEL results showed that apoptosis significantly increased in cKO testes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The absence of SRSF1 causes apoptosis in a large number of spermatogonia that are unable to survive.
source: These data suggested that the absence of SRSF1 causes apoptosis in a large number of spermatogonia that are unable to survive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from TUNEL and VASA staining data.

claim: Partial germ cells could not complete homing in 5 dpp cKO testes.
source: Interestingly, the results of VASA and SOX9 co-staining showed that partial germ cells could not complete homing in 5 dpp cKO testes (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by VASA and SOX9 co-staining data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: In mice, starting at 3 dpp, cytoplasmic FOXO1 in some gonocytes begins to enter the nucleus.
source: In mice, starting at 3 dpp, cytoplasmic FOXO1 in some gonocytes begins to enter the nucleus (Goertz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goertz et al., 2011.

claim: Gonocytes with nuclear FOXO1 further develop into prospermatogonia, which are expected to develop into SSCs.
source: These cells further develop into prospermatogonia, which are expected to develop into SSCs (Goertz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goertz et al., 2011.

claim: There was a reduced number of prospermatogonia in cKO mice.
source: Further, germ cell statistics of FOXO1 expression in the nucleus showed a reduced number of prospermatogonia in cKO mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by FOXO1 immunohistochemical staining and quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Germ cells in which FOXO1 is expressed in the nucleus similarly undergo abnormal homing.
source: And germ cells in which FOXO1 is expressed in the nucleus similarly undergo abnormal homing (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by FOXO1 immunohistochemical staining and quantification data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: SRSF1 has an essential role in the homing of precursor SSCs.
source: Thus, all the above data indicated that SRSF1 has an essential role in the homing of precursor SSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results on homing defects in cKO mice.

claim: The expression of Srsf1 was significantly reduced in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes.
source: RNA-seq and RT-qPCR results showed a significant reduction in the expression of Srsf1 in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SRSF1 expression was significantly reduced in the testes of cKO mice at 5 dpp.
source: Western blotting results showed that SRSF1 expression was significantly reduced in the testes of cKO mice at 5 dpp (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 715 downregulated and 258 upregulated genes were identified by RNA-seq data in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes.
source: The volcano map and cluster heatmap showed 715 downregulated and 258 upregulated genes identified by RNA-seq data in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes (Figure 7C and D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Gene GO enrichment analyses indicated abnormal germ cell development and cell cycle arrest in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes.
source: These gene GO enrichment analyses indicated abnormal germ cell development and cell cycle arrest in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Spermatogonia-associated gene (e.g. Gfra1, Pou5f1, Plzf, Nanos3, Dnd1, Stra8, and Taf4b) expression was significantly reduced in the testes of cKO mice at 5 dpp.
source: Surprisingly, the heatmap showed that spermatogonia-associated gene (e.g. Gfra1, Pou5f1, Plzf, Nanos3, Dnd1, Stra8, and Taf4b) expression was significantly reduced in the testes of cKO mice at 5 dpp (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Germ cell-specific deletion of Srsf1 impairs the expression of spermatogonia-associated genes.
source: Together, these data indicated that germ cell-specific deletion of Srsf1 impairs the expression of spermatogonia-associated genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data.

claim: 3543 of the 4824 genes bound by SRSF1 were expressed in testes at 5 dpp.
source: Considering that the CLIP-seq data were obtained from adult mouse testis, the set of genes bound by CLIP-seq was restricted to those expressed only in the 5 dpp mouse testis RNA-seq data. we found that 3543 of the 4824 genes bound by SRSF1 were expressed in testes at 5 dpp.
evidence: This is based on integration of CLIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 9 out of 715 downregulated genes were bound by SRSF1 and underwent abnormal AS.
source: Venn diagram data revealed that 9 out of 715 downregulated genes were bound by SRSF1 and underwent abnormal AS (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 1 out of 258 upregulated genes was bound by SRSF1 and underwent abnormal AS.
source: And 1 out of 258 upregulated genes was bound by SRSF1 and underwent abnormal AS (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 39 unchanged genes were bound by SRSF1 and underwent abnormal AS.
source: Interestingly, we found that 39 unchanged genes were bound by SRSF1 and underwent abnormal AS (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 162 AS events were significantly affected (false discovery rate [FDR] <0.05) in cKO mouse testes.
source: RNA-seq analyses showed that 162 AS events were significantly affected (false discovery rate [FDR] <0.05) in cKO mouse testes (Figure 8B and C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq AS analysis shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: Most of the 133 affected AS events (162) were classified as skipped exons (SEs), with 10 AS events categorised as retained introns (RIs), 13 as mutually exclusive exons (MXEs), 4 as alternative 5' splice sites (A5SSs), and 2 as alternative 3' splice sites (A3SSs).
source: Most of the 133 affected AS events (162) were classified as skipped exons (SEs), with 10 AS events categorised as retained introns (RIs), 13 as mutually exclusive exons (MXEs), 4 as alternative 5' splice sites (A5SSs), and 2 as alternative 3' splice sites (A3SSs) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by AS analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: SRSF1 effectively inhibits the occurrence of SE and MXE events and promotes the occurrence of RI events.
source: Additionally, the overall analysis of aberrant AS events showed that SRSF1 effectively inhibits the occurrence of SE and MXE events and promotes the occurrence of RI events (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by AS analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Four genes concerning germ cell development were altered in AS forms.
source: Then, GO enrichment analyses of AS genes revealed that four genes concerning germ cell development were altered in AS forms (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Tial1/Tiar affects the survival of primordial germ cells.
source: It has been shown that Tial1/Tiar affects the survival of primordial germ cells (Beck et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Beck et al., 1998.

claim: Tial1/Tiar is 1 of 39 unchanged genes that are bound by SRSF1 and undergo abnormal AS.
source: Moreover, Tial1/Tiar is 1 of 39 unchanged genes that are bound by SRSF1 and undergo abnormal AS.
evidence: This is based on integration of CLIP-seq, RNA-seq, and AS analysis data.

claim: Multiomics analyses suggested that Tial1/Tiar were posttranscriptionally regulated by SRSF1.
source: Thus, multiomics analyses suggested that Tial1/Tiar were posttranscriptionally regulated by SRSF1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiomics analysis.

claim: The pre-mRNA of Tial1/Tiar in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes exhibited abnormal AS.
source: Next, we investigated the mechanism by which SRSF1 regulates the AS of Tial1/Tiar, RT-PCR results showed that the pre-mRNA of Tial1/Tiar in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes exhibited abnormal AS (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: SRSF1 could bind to the pre-mRNA of Tial1/Tiar.
source: The results of RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP)-qPCR showed that SRSF1 could bind to the pre-mRNA of Tial1/Tiar (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by RIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The fragments per kilobase million (FPKM) of Tial1/Tiar was unchanged in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes.
source: Interestingly, RNA-seq analyses showed that the fragments per kilobase million (FPKM) of Tial1/Tiar was unchanged in 5 dpp cKO mouse testes (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Tial1/Tiar transcript levels were not inhibited.
source: RT-qPCR results showed that Tial1/Tiar transcript levels were not inhibited (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Expression levels of TIAL1/TIAR isoform X2 were significantly suppressed.
source: However, western blotting showed that expression levels of TIAL1/TIAR isoform X2 were significantly suppressed (Figure 8J and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: SRSF1 is required for TIAL1/TIAR expression and splicing in spermatogonia survival.
source: In summary, the data indicate that SRSF1 is required for TIAL1/TIAR expression and splicing in spermatogonia survival.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results on Tial1/Tiar regulation.

claim: SRSF1 could interact with AS-related proteins (e.g. SRSF10, SART1, RBM15, SRRM2, SF3B6, and SF3A2).
source: We found that SRSF1 could interact with AS-related proteins (e.g. SRSF10, SART1, RBM15, SRRM2, SF3B6, and SF3A2) (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by IP-MS data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: FLAG-SRSF1 interacted with HA-SART1, HA-RBM15, and HA-SRSF10 in 293T cells.
source: The co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) results indicated that FLAG-SRSF1 interacted with HA-SART1, HA-RBM15, and HA-SRSF10 in 293T cells (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: mCherry-SRSF1 completely co-localised with eGFP-SART1, eGFP-RBM15, and eGFP-SRSF10 in 293T cells.
source: In addition, the fluorescence results showed complete co-localisation of mCherry-SRSF1 with eGFP-SART1, eGFP-RBM15, and eGFP-SRSF10 in 293T cells (Figure 9H).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9H.

claim: The RRM1 domain of SRSF1 interacted with HA-SART1, HA-RBM15, and HA-SRSF10 in 293T cells.
source: Co-IP suggested that the RRM1 domain of SRSF1 interacted with HA-SART1, HA-RBM15, and HA-SRSF10 in 293T cells (Figure 9I).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data with SRSF1 truncated proteins shown in Figure 9I.

claim: SRSF1 may interact with SRSF10, SART1, and RBM15 to regulate AS in 5 dpp mouse testes.
source: Together, the above data show that SRSF1 may interact with SRSF10, SART1, and RBM15 to regulate AS in 5 dpp mouse testes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from IP-MS, Co-IP, and fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: SCOS was observed in Ddx5, Tial1/Tiar, Uhrf1, Pramef12, Dot1l, and Rad51 deletion mouse models.
source: SCOS was observed in Ddx5, Tial1/Tiar, Uhrf1, Pramef12, Dot1l, and Rad51 deletion mouse models (Beck et al., 1998; Legrand et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beck et al., 1998; Legrand et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019; and Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: The absence of germ cells represents classical SCOS in adult mouse testes.
source: The absence of germ cells represents classical SCOS in adult mouse testes (Figure 4; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 and a citation to Wang et al., 2023.

claim: SRSF1 deficiency impairs spermatogonia survival, leading to SCOS in male mice.
source: These data indicate that SRSF1 deficiency impairs spermatogonia survival, leading to SCOS in male mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The earliest event in the development of the SSC population is the migration of prospermatogonia from the centre of seminiferous cords to the basement membrane.
source: The earliest event in the development of the SSC population is the migration of prospermatogonia from the centre of seminiferous cords where they have resided since sex determination of the embryonic gonad to the basement membrane (Oatley and Brinster, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oatley and Brinster, 2012.

claim: Germ cells that do not migrate to the basement membrane are unable to form SSC pools and establish niches.
source: Germ cells that do not migrate to the basement membrane are unable to form SSC pools and establish niches (McLean et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McLean et al., 2003.

claim: SSCs that lose their ecological niche will cease to exist.
source: Germ cells that do not migrate to the basement membrane are unable to form SSC pools and establish niches (McLean et al., 2003). These SSCs that lose their ecological niche will cease to exist.
evidence: This is inferred from the statement about SSCs losing their niche and the subsequent observation of apoptosis.

claim: SRSF1 is crucial for the formation of SSC pools and the establishment of niches through homing of precursor SSCs.
source: In conclusion, SRSF1 is crucial for the formation of SSC pools and the establishment of niches through homing of precursor SSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results on homing defects and germ cell loss in cKO mice.

claim: AS is commonly found in mammals, especially in the brain and testes.
source: AS is commonly found in mammals, especially in the brain and testes (Mazin et al., 2021; Merkin et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mazin et al., 2021; Merkin et al., 2012; and Wang et al., 2008.

claim: AS plays essential roles in the posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression during many developmental processes, such as SSC self-renewal and differentiation.
source: AS plays essential roles in the posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression during many developmental processes, such as SSC self-renewal and differentiation (Chen et al., 2018; Song et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018 and Song et al., 2020.

claim: BUD31-mediated AS of Cdk2 was shown to be required for SSC self-renewal and differentiation.
source: Recently, BUD31-mediated AS of Cdk2 was shown to be required for SSC self-renewal and differentiation (Qin et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Qin et al., 2023.

claim: Srsf10 depletion disturbed the AS of genes, including Nasp, Bclaf1, Rif1, Dazl, Kit, Ret, and Sycp1.
source: Srsf10 depletion disturbed the AS of genes, including Nasp, Bclaf1, Rif1, Dazl, Kit, Ret, and Sycp1 (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: UHRF1 interacts with snRNAs and regulates AS of Tle3 in mouse SSCs.
source: UHRF1 interacts with snRNAs and regulates AS of Tle3 in mouse SSCs (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: Mettl3-mediated m6A regulates AS of Sohlh1 and Dazl.
source: Mettl3-mediated m6A regulates AS of Sohlh1 and Dazl (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2017.

claim: SRSF1 acts as an alternative RNA splicing regulator and directly interacts with Tial1/Tiar transcripts to regulate splicing events in spermatogonia.
source: We found that SRSF1 acts as an alternative RNA splicing regulator and directly interacts with Tial1/Tiar transcripts to regulate splicing events in spermatogonia (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR, RNA-seq, and RIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8E-G.

claim: SRSF1 explicitly regulates the expression of Tial1/Tiar via AS.
source: These results suggested that SRSF1 explicitly regulates the expression of Tial1/Tiar via AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RT-PCR, RNA-seq, RIP-qPCR, and western blotting data.

claim: TIAL1/TIAR is essential for primordial germ cell development in mouse testes.
source: Studies have reported that TIAL1/TIAR is essential for primordial germ cell development in mouse testes (Beck et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Beck et al., 1998.

claim: Tial1/Tiar deletion impairs germ cell survival leading to SCOS.
source: Tial1/Tiar deletion impairs germ cell survival leading to SCOS, consistent with our phenotype (Figures 3E–I–4A–C; Beck et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Beck et al., 1998 and comparison with the phenotype shown in Figures 3E-I and 4A-C.

claim: SRSF1 may affect germ cell survival by directly binding and regulating Tial1/Tiar expression through AS.
source: Taken together, SRSF1 may affect germ cell survival by directly binding and regulating Tial1/Tiar expression through AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results on SRSF1-Tial1/Tiar interaction and regulation.

claim: SRSF10 deficiency impaired spermatogonia differentiation but did not affect homing of precursor SSCs.
source: A recent study reported that SRSF10 deficiency impaired spermatogonia differentiation but did not affect homing of precursor SSCs (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: SRSF1 has a specific function in the homing of precursor SSCs independent of SRSF10.
source: Therefore, this suggests that SRSF1 has a specific function in the homing of precursor SSCs independent of SRSF10.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between SRSF1 and SRSF10 phenotypes.

claim: Aberrant homing of precursor SSCs often lead to gametogenic failure, resulting in subfertility or infertility.
source: Aberrant homing of precursor SSCs often lead to gametogenic failure, resulting in subfertility or infertility (Jiao et al., 2021; Kanatsu-Shinohara and Shinohara, 2013; La and Hobbs, 2019; Song and Wilkinson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiao et al., 2021; Kanatsu-Shinohara and Shinohara, 2013; La and Hobbs, 2019; and Song and Wilkinson, 2014.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in humans and corresponding knockout/mutated mice have been extensively researched.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in humans and corresponding knockout/mutated mice have been extensively researched (Jiao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiao et al., 2021.

claim: AS-related posttranscriptional regulation during meiosis has not been well studied.
source: However, AS-related posttranscriptional regulation during meiosis has not been well studied.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the discussion.

claim: SRSF1 plays a critical role in posttranscriptional regulation to implement homing of precursor SSCs.
source: In summary, this study demonstrates that SRSF1 plays a critical role in posttranscriptional regulation to implement homing of precursor SSCs (Figure 9K).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental results and illustrated in Figure 9K.

claim: The posttranscriptional regulation of SRSF1-mediated splicing is resolved during the formation of SSC pools and the establishment of niches.
source: Thus, the posttranscriptional regulation of SRSF1-mediated splicing is resolved during the formation of SSC pools and the establishment of niches.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.
